1. The animation shows a grid of monthly start dates, running from January 1991 to July 2016. Each square is a month in which someone could have bought a home. Light squares mean the buyer was ahead after ten years. Dark squares mean the renter was ahead. The data sources are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates, and the animation is labeled "illustrative." The idea is that whether buying beats renting depends on when you start. The animation checks that over every possible start month.

2. The first three frames don't visibly change. The grid is almost the same, with a slight shift in camera angle. In frames 4 to 6, a caption appears and stays: "2002 to 2007: 6 of 72 (8.3%)." A highlighted brown column and a lighter strip of squares are also marked. The left, light-colored part of the grid is much larger than the dark part on the right.

3. In most start months, the buyer was ahead after ten years. The caption points to one window, 2002 to 2007, where the buyer came out ahead in only 6 of 72 start months (8.3%). Buyers who started near the mid-2000s peak mostly did worse than renters. The note "US only · history, not a forecast" says these results describe the past. They don't predict the future.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that the timing of a purchase matters, and that buying at a price peak has historically carried more risk. A viewer might also conclude that buying usually beat renting over ten years in this period. But the animation never states either point.

5. None of the advice in 4 comes from the animation. The picture and text show only the data pattern, the 6-of-72 caption and the "history, not a forecast" disclaimer. Any takeaway about when to buy is my own inference.
